name: Nehemiah
sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex, checked against the Septuagint (where Nehemiah forms chapters 11–23 of Esdras B, or 2 Esdras, in Brenton’s public-domain English translation). In the Hebrew Bible, Ezra and Nehemiah were counted as a single book. No scroll of Nehemiah has been securely identified among the Dead Sea Scrolls; a small fragment sometimes assigned to it is disputed. Where the written Hebrew text (ketiv) and the traditional reading (qere) differ, the footnotes give the other reading. Verse numbers follow the standard English Bible; the Hebrew numbers 4:1–6 as 3:33–38, 4:7–23 as 4:1–17, 7:69–73 as 7:68–72, 9:38 as 10:1, and 10:1–39 as 10:2–40. Weights, measures, and money are given in modern US units, and calendar dates with their modern-month equivalents, with the originals and metric figures in the footnotes. Dates BC are approximate.

verses.text: The words of Nehemiah{a} son of Hacaliah. In the month of Chislev (November–December),{b} in the twentieth year,{c} I was in Susa the citadel.{d}
Hanani, one of my brothers, came with some men from Judah, and I asked them about the Jews who had escaped, those who had survived the captivity, and about Jerusalem.

And they said to me, “The survivors who remained from the captivity there in the province are in great trouble and disgrace. The wall of Jerusalem is broken through, and its gates have been burned with fire.”
When I heard these words, I sat down and wept, and I mourned for days, and I kept fasting and praying before the God of heaven.
I said, “Yahweh, God of heaven, great and awesome God, you keep your covenant and show faithful love to those who love you and obey your commands.

Please look at me and listen to the prayer your servant is praying to you today, day and night, for your servants the people of Israel. I confess the sins we Israelites have committed against you. Both I and my family have sinned.
We have dealt very corruptly with you; we have not kept the commandments, the statutes, or the ordinances that you gave to your servant Moses.
Remember, please, the word that you commanded Moses your servant: ‘If you act unfaithfully, I will scatter you among the peoples;

but if you turn back to me and obey my commands, then even if your scattered people are at the farthest reaches of the sky, I will gather them from there and bring them{e} to the place I have chosen as a dwelling for my name.’{f}
They are your servants and your people, whom you redeemed by your great power and by your strong hand.

Lord,{g} please listen to the prayer of your servant and to the prayer of all your servants who take joy in revering your name. Give your servant success today, and make this man show him mercy.” At that time I was the king’s cupbearer.{h}

notes.text: Nehemiah means “Yahweh comforts.” In the Hebrew Bible, Ezra and Nehemiah were counted as one book. In the Septuagint they form a single book, Esdras B (2 Esdras), of which Nehemiah is chapters 11–23; in the Latin Vulgate, Nehemiah is called 2 Esdras (and sometimes the Second Book of Ezra), while Ezra is 1 Esdras.
Hebrew Kislev, the ninth month, which fell in November–December. The written text (ketiv) spells it Kislo.
The twentieth year of Artaxerxes I (2:1), that is, late 446 BC.
Susa (Hebrew Shushan), the winter capital of the Persian kings, in southwestern Iran. The “citadel” (birah) was the fortified royal quarter.
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has a variant spelling of the same verb.
See Leviticus 26:33; Deuteronomy 4:27; 12:5; 30:1–4.
Hebrew Adonai.
The cupbearer tasted and served the king’s wine and was a trusted official with close access to the king.

verses.text: In the month of Nisan (March–April),{a} in the twentieth year of King Artaxerxes,{b} wine was set before him, and I took it and handed it to the king. I had never been sad in his presence before.
The king asked me, “Why do you look so sad, when you are not ill? This can only be sorrow of the heart.” I was terrified.
And I answered the king, “May the king live forever! How could my face not be sad, when the city where my fathers are buried lies waste and its gates are eaten up with fire?”
The king said to me, “For what are you asking?” And I prayed to the God of heaven.
I answered the king, “If it please the king, and if your servant has gained your favor, send me to Judah, to the city where my ancestors are buried, so that I can rebuild it.”
Then the king, with the queen{c} seated beside him, asked me, “How long will your trip take, and when will you come back?” It pleased the king to send me, so I named a time.
And I said to the king, “If it pleases the king, let letters be given me to the governors of the province Beyond the River,{d} that they may let me pass through until I come to Judah,

and a letter to Asaph, who keeps the king’s park,{e} directing him to give me timber for beams for the gates of the citadel beside the temple, for the city wall, and for the house I am to occupy.” And the king gave me these things, because the good hand of my God was on me.
Then I came to the governors of the province Beyond the River and gave them the king’s letters. Now the king had sent with me officers of the army and horsemen.
When Sanballat the Horonite{f} and Tobiah the servant, the Ammonite,{g} heard of it, it was a great evil in their eyes that a man had come to seek good for the sons of Israel.
So I came to Jerusalem and was there three days.
I got up during the night, along with a few men. I told no one what my God had put in my heart to do for Jerusalem. I took no animal except the one I was riding.

That night I went out through the Valley Gate toward the Dragon Spring{h} and the Dung Gate, examining the walls of Jerusalem, which were broken down,{i} and its gates, which had been destroyed by fire.
Then I passed on to the Fountain Gate and the King’s Pool, but there was no space for the beast I rode to get through.
So I went up the valley{j} during the night, examining the wall. Then I turned back and came in again through the Valley Gate.
The officials had no knowledge of where I went or what I did, for up to then I had told nothing to the Jews, to the priests, nobles, and officials, or to the rest who were to do the work.
Then I told them, “You can see the trouble we are in: Jerusalem is a ruin, and its gates have been burned. Come, let us rebuild the wall of Jerusalem and put an end to our disgrace.”
I told them how kindly my God’s hand had been on me, and what the king had said to me. They answered, “Let’s start building!” And they set their hands to the good work.
But Sanballat the Horonite, Tobiah the Ammonite official, and Geshem the Arab{k} heard about it and ridiculed and scorned us. “What are you doing?” they asked. “Are you rebelling against the king?”
I replied, “The God of heaven will make us prosper. We are his servants, and we will begin to build. But you have no share, claim, or historic right in Jerusalem.”

notes.text: Hebrew Nisan, the first month, which fell in March–April; here spring 445 BC.
Artaxerxes I Longimanus, king of Persia 465–424 BC.
Hebrew shegal, a royal consort, perhaps the chief queen.
The Persian province west of the Euphrates, which included Syria and Judah.
Hebrew pardes, a Persian loanword for a park or enclosed royal woodland; it is the source of the word “paradise.”
Sanballat (Babylonian Sin-uballiṭ, “Sin [the moon god] has given life”) was governor of Samaria, as the Elephantine papyri show. “Horonite” probably means from Beth-horon.
Or “official.” Tobiah means “Yahweh is good”; he was probably governor of Ammon, east of the Jordan.
Or “Jackal Spring.”
So the traditional reading (qere), “which they were broken down”; the written text (ketiv) has a different form of the same verb.
The Kidron Valley, east of the city.
Geshem (Arabic Jashm) is known from an inscribed silver bowl as a king of Kedar, a powerful Arab confederation in the northern Arabian desert.

verses.text: Eliashib the high priest and his fellow priests set to work and rebuilt the Sheep Gate. They consecrated it and set up its doors, consecrating the wall as far as the Tower of the Hundred{a} and the Tower of Hananel.
Next to him the men of Jericho built. And next to them Zaccur son of Imri built.
The sons of Hassenaah built the Fish Gate. They laid its beams and set up its doors, its bolts, and its bars.
At their hand Meremoth son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz, repaired. At his hand Meshullam son of Berechiah, son of Meshezabel, repaired. At his hand Zadok son of Baana repaired.
And next to them the Tekoites made repairs, but their nobles would not bend their necks to the work of their lords.{b}
Joiada son of Paseah and Meshullam son of Besodeiah repaired the Old Gate.{c} They laid its beams and set up its doors, its bolts, and its bars.
And next to them Melatiah the Gibeonite and Jadon the Meronothite, the men of Gibeon and of Mizpah, made repairs, up to the seat of the governor of the province Beyond the River.{d}
At his hand Uzziel son of Harhaiah, of the goldsmiths, repaired; and at his hand Hananiah, a member of the perfumers, repaired. They left{e} Jerusalem whole up to the Broad Wall.
At their hand Rephaiah son of Hur, who governed half the district of Jerusalem, repaired.
At their hand Jedaiah son of Harumaph repaired, across from his house; and at his hand Hattush son of Hashabneiah repaired.
A second section, together with the Tower of the Ovens, was repaired by Malchijah son of Harim and Hasshub son of Pahath-moab.
At his hand Shallum son of Hallohesh, who governed half the district of Jerusalem, repaired, together with his daughters.
The Valley Gate was repaired by Hanun and the people living in Zanoah. They built it and hung its doors with their bolts and bars, and repaired 1,500 feet{f} of wall up to the Dung Gate.
Malchijah son of Rechab, ruler of the district of Beth-haccherem, repaired the Dung Gate. He rebuilt it and set up its doors, its bolts, and its bars.

Shallun son of Col-hozeh, ruler of the district of Mizpah, repaired the Fountain Gate. He rebuilt it, covered it with a roof, and set up its doors{g} with their bolts and bars. He also repaired the wall of the Pool of Shelah{h} by the king’s garden, as far as the stairs that descend from the City of David.
After him Nehemiah son of Azbuk, who governed half the district of Beth-zur, repaired up to a point across from David’s tombs, to the pool that had been made, and to the House of the Warriors.
After him the Levites repaired: Rehum son of Bani; at his hand Hashabiah, who governed half the district of Keilah, repaired for his own district.
After him their brothers made repairs: Bavvai{i} son of Henadad, ruler of half the district of Keilah.
At his hand Ezer son of Jeshua, who governed Mizpah, repaired a second section, across from the way up to the armory at the Angle.
After him Baruch son of Zabbai{j} worked eagerly{k} on a second section, from the Angle to the doorway of the house of Eliashib the high priest.
After him Meremoth son of Uriah, son of Hakkoz, repaired a second section, from the doorway of Eliashib’s house to where Eliashib’s house ended.
After him the priests, the men of the surrounding district,{l} made repairs.
After them Benjamin and Hasshub made repairs opposite their house. After them Azariah son of Maaseiah, son of Ananiah, made repairs beside his own house.
After him Binnui son of Henadad repaired a second section, from Azariah’s house up to the Angle and the corner.
Palal son of Uzai worked on the section opposite the Angle and the tower that stands out from the upper house of the king, beside the court of the guard. Next in line came Pedaiah son of Parosh
while the temple servants who lived on the Ophel{m} repaired up to a point across from the Water Gate toward the east and the tower that juts out.
After them the men of Tekoa repaired a second section, across from the great tower that juts out, up to the wall of the Ophel.
From above the Horse Gate the priests repaired, every man across from his own house.
After them Zadok son of Immer repaired across from his house; after him Shemaiah son of Shecaniah, keeper of the East Gate, repaired.
After him{n} Hananiah son of Shelemiah and Hanun, Zalaph’s sixth son, repaired a second section. After him Meshullam son of Berechiah repaired across from his own room.
After him Malchijah, a member of the goldsmiths, repaired up to the house of the temple servants and the traders, across from the Muster Gate,{o} and up to the corner’s upper room.
And between the upper room of the corner and the Sheep Gate the goldsmiths and the merchants made repairs.

notes.text: Hebrew the Tower of Hammeah. Its name may refer to its height of a hundred cubits (about 150 feet or 45 meters) or to a hundred steps.
Or “their Lord.”
Or “the Jeshanah Gate,” naming the town of Jeshanah, toward which it faced.
The meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain; possibly “who were under the jurisdiction of the governor.”
The meaning of the Hebrew verb is uncertain; usually “left,” here perhaps “paved” or “restored.”
Hebrew “a thousand cubits,” about 1,500 feet or 450 meters.
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has “and they set up.”
Shelah, “channel,” is the pool fed by Hezekiah’s tunnel, called Siloam (Shiloah) in Isaiah 8:6 and John 9:7.
Some Hebrew manuscripts and the Septuagint and Syriac have Binnui (see verse 24).
So the written text (ketiv); the traditional reading (qere) is Zaccai.
Hebrew heḥerah, literally “burned,” that is, with zeal. The word is uncertain and may have arisen by copying; the Septuagint lacks it.
Hebrew kikkar, “circle,” the Jordan Valley around Jericho, or the region around Jerusalem.
The Ophel (“swelling,” “hill”) was the ridge between the City of David and the temple mount.
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has “after me.” Likewise in verse 31.
Or “the Inspection Gate”; Hebrew the Miphkad Gate.

verses.text: When Sanballat heard that we were rebuilding the wall, he became furious and was deeply angered. He ridiculed the Jews,{a}

He spoke before his brothers and the army of Samaria and said, “What are these weak Jews up to? Will they leave it to themselves? Will they offer sacrifice? Will they be done in a day? Will they bring the stones back to life out of the rubbish heaps, burned stones at that?”
And Tobiah the Ammonite, standing beside him, said, “Let them build—if a fox climbed on that stone wall of theirs, it would break it down!”
Hear us, our God, for we are scorned! Bring their insults back on their own heads, and hand them over as spoil in a land where they are captives.
Do not cover over their guilt, and do not let their sin be wiped away before you, for they have insulted you in front of the builders.{b}
So we built the wall, and all the wall was joined together up to half its height, for the people had a heart to work.

But when it came to the ears of Sanballat and Tobiah, the Arabs, the Ammonites, and the Ashdodites that healing had come to the walls of Jerusalem and that the gaps had begun to close, their anger blazed.
And they all plotted together to come and fight against Jerusalem and to cause confusion in it.
And we prayed to our God, and because of them we posted a watch against them by day and by night.
Meanwhile the people of Judah were saying, “The laborers are growing weak, and there is so much rubble that we cannot work on the wall.”
And our enemies said, “They will not know or see until we come into their midst and kill them and stop the work.”
Then the Jews who lived near them kept coming and warning us again and again, “They will attack us from every place you turn.”{c}
So in the lowest parts of the space behind the wall, in the open places,{d} I stationed the people by their families, with their swords, their spears, and their bows.

After looking things over, I stood up and said to the nobles, the officials, and the rest of the people, “Do not be afraid of them. Remember the Lord,{e} who is great and awesome, and fight for your relatives, your sons and daughters, your wives, and your homes.”
Once our enemies heard that we knew of it, and that God had broken up their plan, all of us went back{f} to the wall, every man to his own task.
From then on, half of my young men did the work while half of them held the spears, the shields, the bows, and the armor; and the officers stood behind all the house of Judah
who were building the wall. The men carrying loads did their work with one hand, while the other hand held a weapon.
Every builder worked with his sword fastened at his waist, and the trumpeter stood next to me.
Then I said to the nobles, the officials, and the rest of the people, “The work is large and spread out, and we are far apart from one another along the wall.
Wherever you hear the trumpet blast, gather to us at that spot. Our God will fight for us.”
So we went on with the work, half of them holding spears, from first light until the stars appeared.
At that time I also told the people, “Every man and his servant must spend the night inside Jerusalem. Then they can serve as our guard at night and as workers by day.”
So none of us—not I, not my brothers, not my young men, not the guardsmen behind me—took off our clothes; each one kept his weapon at his right hand.{g}

notes.text: In the Hebrew text, verses 1–6 of this chapter are numbered 3:33–38, and verses 7–23 are numbered 4:1–17. This translation follows the verse numbering of the standard English Bible. The Septuagint follows the Hebrew numbering.
Or “they have hurled insults in front of the builders.”
The meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain.
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has a variant spelling.
Hebrew Adonai.
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has “and we will return.”
The meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain; literally “each his weapon, the water.”

verses.text: Then a great cry went up from the people and their wives against their brothers the Jews.
Some were saying, “We and our sons and daughters are many. We must get grain to eat so that we can survive.”
Others said, “We are putting up our fields, vineyards, and houses as security to get grain during the famine.”
Others said, “We have had to borrow silver to pay the king’s tribute on our fields and vineyards.

We are the same flesh and blood as our fellow Israelites, and our children are as good as theirs. Yet we are forcing our sons and daughters into slavery. Some of our daughters are already enslaved, and we are powerless to stop it, because other men now own our fields and vineyards.”
I was very angry when I heard their outcry and these words.
I thought it over and then brought charges against the nobles and officials. I told them, “You are charging interest{a} to your own people!” I also called a large assembly against them

and I told them, “As far as was in our power, we have redeemed our brothers the Jews who were sold to the nations—and now you yourselves sell your brothers, so that they must be sold back to us?” They kept quiet and found nothing to answer.
And I said,{b} “What you do is not good. Should you not walk in the fear of our God, so that the nations, our enemies, have no cause to reproach us?
I too, and my brothers and my young men, have been lending them silver and grain. Let us give up this lending on interest.
Give back to them, today, their fields, vineyards, olive orchards, and houses, and the percentage{c} on the silver, grain, new wine, and oil that you have been charging them.”
They answered, “We will give it back and demand nothing of them; we will do just what you say.” Then I summoned the priests and put the men under oath to keep this promise.

I shook out the front of my robe as well and said, “Thus may God shake out of his house and out of the fruit of his labor every man who does not carry out this word; thus may he be shaken out and left empty.” And all the assembly said, “Amen,” and praised Yahweh. And the people kept this word.

Furthermore, from the day I was appointed their governor in the land of Judah, from the twentieth year until the thirty-second year of King Artaxerxes{d} (twelve years), neither I nor my relatives drew the governor’s food allowance.

The governors before me had weighed down the people and taken bread and wine from them, as well as about a pound of silver.{e} Their young men also domineered over the people. But I did not act like that, because I feared God.
Instead, I devoted myself to the work on this wall. We bought no land, and all my servants were gathered there to work.
There were at my table, besides, 150 Jews and officials, not counting those who came to us from the surrounding nations.

What was made ready daily at my cost was one ox and six choice sheep, and fowl as well, and once every ten days a great supply of all kinds of wine. Even so, I never asked for the bread of the governor, because the labor weighed heavily on this people.
O my God, remember me for good, for all I have done for this people.

notes.text: So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has a variant spelling. The meaning is “lending on pledge,” or “taking interest.”
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has “and he said.”
Hebrew “the hundredth,” probably a charge of one percent a month, or twelve percent a year.
From 445 to 433 BC.
Hebrew “40 shekels of silver,” about 1 pound (460 grams), probably a daily charge.

verses.text: When Sanballat, Tobiah, Geshem the Arab, and the rest of our enemies heard that I had rebuilt the wall and that not a gap remained in it (though I had not yet set up the doors in the gates),
Sanballat and Geshem sent me this message: “Come, let us meet with one another at Hakkephirim{a} in the plain of Ono.” But they were planning to do me evil.
And I sent messengers to them, saying, “I am doing a great work and I cannot come down. Why should the work stop while I leave it and come down to you?”
They sent me word in this manner four times, and four times I answered them in the same manner.
Then a fifth time Sanballat sent his young man to me in the same way, carrying an unsealed letter.

It said: “A rumor is going around among the nations, and Gashmu{b} says it is true, that you and the Jews are plotting to rebel, and that this is why you are building the wall. According to these reports, you are going to become their king.
You have even appointed prophets to announce in Jerusalem about you, ‘There is a king in Judah!’ Now these reports will reach the king. So come now, and let us consult with each other.”
I sent back to him, “Nothing has happened like what you are saying; you are making it up in your own mind.”
They were all trying to scare us, thinking, “They will lose heart for the work, and it will never be finished.” But now, strengthen my hands!{c}

Then I went to the house of Shemaiah son of Delaiah, son of Mehetabel, who was shut in. He said, “Let us meet at the house of God, inside the temple, and shut the temple doors; for they are coming to kill you—by night they are coming to kill you.”
I replied, “Should a man like me flee? And who that is such as I could enter the temple and keep his life?{d} I will not go in.”
Then I perceived that God had not sent him at all; he had spoken this prophecy against me because Tobiah and Sanballat had paid him.
He had been paid so that I would take fright, act this way, and sin; then they would have an evil report with which to reproach me.
Remember, my God, what Tobiah and Sanballat have done, and also the prophetess Noadiah and the rest of the prophets who kept trying to intimidate me.
So the wall was finished on the twenty-fifth day of the month Elul (August–September),{e} in fifty-two days.
When all our enemies heard, all the nations surrounding us were afraid and were greatly cast down in their own eyes, for they knew that this work had been done by our God.
Moreover, in those days the nobles of Judah sent many letters to Tobiah, and Tobiah’s letters came to them.
For there were many in Judah sworn to him, since he was son-in-law to Shecaniah son of Arah, and Jehohanan his son had married the daughter of Meshullam son of Berechiah.
They also kept telling me of his good deeds, and they carried my words out to him. And Tobiah sent letters to frighten me.

notes.text: Or “in one of the villages.”
Gashmu is another form of the name Geshem.
A brief prayer; the Hebrew does not name God here. The Septuagint reads “And now I strengthened my hands.”
Nehemiah was not a priest; for a layman to enter the temple building was forbidden (Numbers 18:7).

Hebrew Elul, the sixth month, which fell in August–September; in 445 BC its twenty-fifth day fell about the beginning of October. Fifty-two days of work means the building began early in the fifth month, Av (July–August).

verses.text: When the wall was built and I had hung the doors, and the gatekeepers, the singers, and the Levites were appointed,
I put Jerusalem in the charge of Hanani my brother and of Hananiah, the commander of the citadel, for he was a faithful man who feared God beyond many.

And I said{a} to them, “The gates of Jerusalem must stay closed until the sun is hot; while the gatekeepers stand at their posts, have them close the doors and fasten them. And set watches drawn from those who live in Jerusalem, every man at his station and every man in front of his house.”
Now the city was broad and large, with few people in it, and the houses had not been built.

And my God put it into my heart to bring together the nobles, the officials, and the people, to enroll them by their genealogy. I came upon the register of the genealogy of those who came up at the beginning, and I found in it this record:{b}
These are the people of the province who came back from captivity in exile, the ones King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon had deported. They returned to Jerusalem and Judah, each to his own town.
They came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Azariah,{c} Raamiah, Nahamani, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispereth, Bigvai, Nehum, Baanah. The number of the men of the people of Israel:

The temple servants together with the sons of Solomon’s servants totaled 392.
And these went up from Tel-melah, Tel-harsha, Cherub, Addon, and Immer, but they were unable to show their fathers’ house and their lineage, whether they were of Israel:
the sons of Delaiah, of Tobiah, and of Nekoda, 642.
And from the priests: the descendants of Hobaiah, Hakkoz, and Barzillai (this man had married one of the daughters of Barzillai the Gileadite and taken their name).
These searched for their entry among those enrolled in the genealogies, but it was not found, and so they were barred from the priesthood as unclean.
The governor{e} told them that they were not to eat any of the most holy food until a priest should arise to consult the Urim and Thummim.
The whole assembly together was 42,360,
besides their male and female servants, who were 7,337. And they had 245 singing men and singing women.
Their horses were 736, their mules 245,{f}
their camels 435, and their donkeys 6,720.
Some of the family heads contributed to the work. The governor gave the treasury 1,000 gold darics (about 18½ pounds of gold),{g} 50 bowls, and 530 priestly garments.
Some of the family heads gave the treasury for the work 20,000 gold darics (about 370 pounds of gold){h} and about 1⅓ tons of silver.{i}
And what the rest of the people gave was 20,000 gold darics (about 370 pounds of gold), about 1¼ tons of silver,{j} and 67 priests’ garments.

The priests, Levites, gatekeepers, singers, some of the people, the temple servants, and all the rest of Israel settled in their own towns. When the seventh month (September–October){k} arrived, the Israelites were living in their towns.

notes.text: So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has “and he said.”
Verses 6–73 repeat Ezra 2:1–70 with many small differences in names and numbers.
Ezra 2:2 has Seraiah, Reelaiah, Mispar, and Rehum for Azariah, Raamiah, Mispereth, and Nehum, and lacks Nahamani.
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has Nephushsim.
Hebrew Tirshatha, a Persian title, perhaps “His Excellency.” See Ezra 2:63.
This verse is lacking in most Hebrew manuscripts; it is supplied from some manuscripts and from Ezra 2:66. As a result, verses 69–73 in this translation are numbered 68–72 in the Hebrew.
Hebrew darkemonim, the Persian gold daric (or perhaps the Greek drachma). A daric weighed about 0.3 ounce (8.4 grams), so 1,000 darics weighed about 8.4 kilograms.
That is, about 168 kilograms.
Hebrew “2,200 minas of silver.” A mina was about 1¼ pounds (575 grams), so 2,200 minas is about 2,750 pounds (1,265 kilograms).
Hebrew “2,000 minas of silver,” about 2,500 pounds (1,150 kilograms).
Hebrew “the seventh month,” Tishri, which fell in September–October; here the autumn of 445 BC.

verses.text: All the people assembled together in the square in front of the Water Gate. They asked Ezra the scribe to bring out the Book of the Law of Moses, which Yahweh had given to Israel.{a}
So on the first day of the seventh month (September–October),{b} Ezra the priest brought the Law before the assembly of men and women and everyone able to understand what they heard.

He read in it before the square in front of the Water Gate from first light until midday, before the men and women and all who could understand; and all the people listened closely to the Book of the Law.

Ezra the scribe stood on a wooden platform{c} made for this purpose. Beside him on his right stood Mattithiah, Shema, Anaiah, Uriah, Hilkiah, and Maaseiah; and on his left stood Pedaiah, Mishael, Malchijah, Hashum, Hashbaddanah, Zechariah, and Meshullam.
And Ezra opened the book in the sight of all the people, for he was above all the people, and as he opened it all the people stood.
And Ezra blessed Yahweh, the great God, and all the people answered, “Amen, Amen,” lifting up their hands. And they bowed their heads and worshiped Yahweh with their faces to the ground.

Jeshua, Bani, Sherebiah, Jamin, Akkub, Shabbethai, Hodiah, Maaseiah, Kelita, Azariah, Jozabad, Hanan, and Pelaiah—the Levites—were explaining the Law to the people, as the people stood in their places.
They read in the book, in the Law of God, distinctly,{d} and they gave the meaning, and made the reading understood.

Then Nehemiah the governor,{e} Ezra the priest and scribe, and the Levites who were teaching the people told everyone, “This day is holy to Yahweh your God. Do not mourn or weep.” The people had all been weeping as they heard the words of the Law.
Nehemiah said, “Go and enjoy rich food and sweet drinks, and send some to anyone who has nothing ready, since this day is holy to our Lord.{f} Do not be sad, for the joy of Yahweh is your strength.”
The Levites, too, were quieting all the people and saying, “Hush, for the day is holy; do not grieve.”
Then all the people went off to eat and drink, to send portions to others, and to celebrate with great joy, because they had grasped the words that were explained to them.
On the second day, the heads of families from among all the people, together with the priests and Levites, gathered around Ezra the scribe to study the words of the Law.
And they found it written in the Law that Yahweh had commanded by Moses that the sons of Israel should dwell in booths during the feast of the seventh month,{g}

and that they were to announce and spread the word through all their towns and in Jerusalem: “Go out to the hill country and fetch boughs of olive and of wild olive, of myrtle and palm and other leafy trees, to make booths, as it is written.”

So the people went out and brought branches and built themselves booths, each on his own roof, in their courtyards, in the courtyards of God’s house, and in the squares by the Water Gate and the Gate of Ephraim.

So the whole assembly who had come back from the captivity made booths and dwelt in them; for since the days of Jeshua{h} son of Nun until that day the sons of Israel had not done it. And the joy was exceedingly great.
And day by day, from the first day to the last day, he read from the Book of the Law of God. They kept the feast seven days, and on the eighth day there was a solemn assembly, according to the rule.

notes.text: Nehemiah 7:73b–8:12 is retold in the Greek book 1 Esdras (9:37–55), which ends with this scene.
Hebrew “the first day of the seventh month,” the day of trumpet blasts (Leviticus 23:24), which later became the Jewish New Year (Rosh Hashanah).
Hebrew “a tower of wood.”
Or “with interpretation,” perhaps meaning that the Hebrew was explained or translated into Aramaic, the everyday language of the time.
Hebrew Tirshatha, a Persian title; see Ezra 2:63.
Hebrew Adonai.
See Leviticus 23:33–43. The Feast of Booths (Sukkot, or Tabernacles) began on the fifteenth day of the seventh month (September–October).
Jeshua is a later form of the name Joshua.

verses.text: On the twenty-fourth day of this month (in September–October){a} the sons of Israel gathered, fasting, wearing sackcloth, with dust upon them.
And the offspring of Israel separated themselves from all foreigners and stood and confessed their sins and the iniquities of their fathers.
And they stood up in their place and read from the Book of the Law of Yahweh their God for about three hours;{b} for another three hours they made confession and worshiped Yahweh their God.
On the stairs of the Levites stood Jeshua, Bani, Kadmiel, Shebaniah, Bunni, Sherebiah, Bani, and Chenani, and they called out loudly to Yahweh their God.

Then the Levites, Jeshua, Kadmiel, Bani, Hashabneiah, Sherebiah, Hodiah, Shebaniah, and Pethahiah, said, “Stand up and bless Yahweh your God from everlasting to everlasting. Blessed be your glorious name, which is exalted above all blessing and praise.

“You alone are Yahweh.{c} You made the heavens, even the highest heavens, with all their host; the earth and everything on it; the seas and everything in them. You give life to all of them, and the host of heaven bows down to you.
You are Yahweh God, who chose Abram, brought him out from Ur of the Chaldeans, and named him Abraham.{d}

You found his heart faithful toward you and cut a covenant with him to give the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Jebusites, and Girgashites—to give it to his seed. And you have fulfilled your words, because you are righteous.
“And you saw the affliction of our fathers in Egypt and heard their cry at the Red Sea,{e}

You gave signs and wonders against Pharaoh, against all his servants, and against all the people of his land, for you knew how proudly they dealt with them; and you made yourself a name that remains to this day.
And you divided the sea before them, so that they went through the midst of the sea on dry land, and you cast their pursuers into the depths, as a stone into mighty waters.
By a pillar of cloud you led them by day, and by a pillar of fire by night, to light for them the way in which they should go.
You came down on Mount Sinai and spoke with them from heaven. You gave them just rulings and true laws, and good decrees and commands.
You made your holy Sabbath known to them, and through your servant Moses you gave them commands, decrees, and a law.

When they were hungry you gave them bread from heaven, and when they were thirsty you brought them water from the rock. You told them to go in and take over the land you had promised with an oath to give them.
“But they, our fathers, behaved proudly; they hardened their necks and would not listen to your commandments.

They would not listen; they did not call to mind your wonders that you had done among them, but hardened their necks and in their rebellion set up a head to go back to their bondage.{f} But you are a God of pardons, gracious and compassionate, long-suffering and great in steadfast love,{g} and you did not abandon them.
Even when they cast for themselves an image of a calf and said, ‘This is your God, who brought you up out of Egypt,’ and committed terrible blasphemies,

you did not abandon them in the desert, because of your great compassion. By day the pillar of cloud did not leave them but guided them on their path, and by night the pillar of fire lit up the way they were to go.
You gave your good Spirit to teach them. You did not hold back your manna from their mouths, and you gave them water when they were thirsty.
For forty years you fed them in the wilderness; they wanted for nothing. Their garments did not wear out, and their feet did not swell.
You gave them kingdoms and peoples and parceled them out as a border.{h} They took the land of Sihon—that is,{i} the land of the king of Heshbon—and the land of Og king of Bashan as their own.
You made their sons as many as the stars of the sky, and you brought them into the land of which you had told their fathers that they would go in to possess it.

So their descendants entered and took possession of the land. You subdued the Canaanites who lived there and handed them over to your people, along with their kings and the peoples of the land, to deal with as they wished.

They took strong cities and fertile ground, and came to own houses filled with every good thing, cisterns dug out, vineyards, olive groves, and fruit trees in plenty. They ate, were satisfied, grew fat, and reveled in your great goodness.
“Yet they disobeyed and rebelled against you; they threw your law behind their backs and killed your prophets, who testified against them to bring them back to you; and they committed great contempt.

So you handed them over to their foes, who oppressed them. In their time of distress they cried to you, and you heard from heaven, and in your great compassion you gave them saviors to save them out of the hand of their foes.

Yet as soon as they had relief, they went back to doing evil before you. So you abandoned them to their enemies, who ruled over them. Again they cried out to you, and from heaven you heard and delivered them, time after time, in your compassion.

You testified against them to bring them back to your law, but they acted proudly and would not listen to your commandments; they sinned against your ordinances, by which a man who does them shall live.{j} They turned away a defiant shoulder, hardened their necks, and would not listen.
For many years you put up with them and warned them by your Spirit through your prophets, but they would not pay attention. So you gave them into the hands of the peoples around them.
Yet in your abundant compassion you did not make a full end of them or abandon them, for you are a God gracious and compassionate.

“And now, our God, great, mighty, and awesome God, who keeps covenant and faithful love: do not let all the hardship that has come on us seem small to you, on our kings, our officials, our priests, our prophets, our ancestors, and all your people, from the time of the kings of Assyria until today.
You are in the right in all that has come on us; you have acted in faithfulness, while we have done wickedly.
Our kings, our officials, our priests, and our fathers have not done your law, nor heeded your commandments and the testimonies with which you warned them.
In their kingdom, with the great goodness you gave them, and in the broad and fertile land you put before them, they did not serve you, nor did they turn back from their evil deeds.
Look—today we are slaves, slaves in the very land you gave our fathers to eat its fruit and its good things.
Its plentiful harvest belongs to the kings whom you set over us because of our sins; they have power over our bodies and our cattle at their pleasure, and we are in great distress.
“For all this we are making a sure agreement and writing it, and on the sealed copy are our officials, our Levites, and our priests.”{k}

notes.text: Hebrew “the twenty-fourth day of this month,” the seventh month, Tishri, two days after the close of the Feast of Booths.
Hebrew “a quarter of the day.” The daylight hours were about twelve, so a quarter was about three hours.
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has a shorter spelling of “you.” The Septuagint begins the verse “And Ezra said.”
Abram means “exalted father”; Abraham was understood as “father of a multitude” (Genesis 17:5).
Hebrew Yam Suph, “Sea of Reeds.”
So the traditional Hebrew text. Some Hebrew manuscripts and the Septuagint read “in Egypt,” that is, “set up a head to return to their bondage in Egypt” (compare Numbers 14:4).
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has “and steadfast love.”
Or “allotted them as a boundary.”
Or “and.”
See Leviticus 18:5.
In the Hebrew text this verse is 10:1, and 10:1–39 is numbered 10:2–40.

verses.text: On the seals were the names of{a} Nehemiah the governor, the son of Hacaliah, and Zedekiah,
Seraiah, Azariah, and Jeremiah,
Pashhur, Amariah, and Malchijah,
Hattush, Shebaniah, and Malluch,
Harim, Meremoth, and Obadiah,
Daniel, Ginnethon, and Baruch,
Meshullam, Abijah, and Mijamin,
Maaziah, Bilgai, and Shemaiah. These were the priests.
And the Levites: Jeshua son of Azaniah, Binnui of the sons of Henadad, Kadmiel;
and their relatives Shebaniah, Hodiah, Kelita, Pelaiah, and Hanan,
Mica, Rehob, and Hashabiah,
Zaccur, Sherebiah, and Shebaniah,
Hodiah, Bani, and Beninu.
The leaders of the people: Parosh, Pahath-moab, Elam, Zattu, and Bani,
Bunni, Azgad, and Bebai,
Adonijah, Bigvai, and Adin,
Ater, Hezekiah, and Azzur,
Hodiah, Hashum, and Bezai,
Hariph, Anathoth, and Nebai,{b}
Magpiash, Meshullam, and Hezir,
Meshezabel, Zadok, and Jaddua,
Pelatiah, Hanan, and Anaiah,
Hoshea, Hananiah, and Hasshub,
Hallohesh, Pilha, and Shobek,
Rehum, Hashabnah, and Maaseiah,
Ahiah, Hanan, and Anan,
Malluch, Harim, and Baanah.

The rest of the people, including the priests, Levites, gatekeepers, singers, temple servants, and all who had separated themselves from the surrounding peoples to follow the Law of God, along with their wives and all their sons and daughters who were old enough to understand,

they hold fast with their brothers, their nobles, and come under a curse and an oath to walk in the Law of God given through Moses, God’s servant, and to keep and perform every commandment of Yahweh our Lord,{c} with his ordinances and statutes.
We will not give our daughters to the peoples of the land or take their daughters for our sons.

If the peoples of the land bring wares or grain of any sort on the day of the Sabbath to sell, we will buy none of it from them on a Sabbath or holy day. We will also let the seventh year lie fallow and give up the claim on every debt.{d}
We also accept the responsibility of giving each year an eighth of an ounce of silver{e} toward the service of the house of our God:

for the bread of the Presence, for the continual grain offering and the continual burnt offering, for the Sabbaths, new moons, and set feasts, for the holy offerings and the sin offerings that make atonement for Israel, and for every task of the house of our God.

We have also cast lots among the priests, Levites, and people for the wood offering, to bring it to the house of our God at set times each year, by our family groups, to burn on the altar of Yahweh our God, as the Law prescribes.
We obligate ourselves to bring the firstfruits of our ground and the firstfruits of all fruit of every tree, year by year, to the house of Yahweh;

also to bring to the house of our God, to the priests who minister in the house of our God, the firstborn of our sons and of our livestock, as it is written in the Law, and the firstborn of our herds and of our flocks;

We will also bring the first batch of our dough{f} and our contributions, the fruit of every kind of tree, the new wine, and the oil to the priests, at the storerooms of the house of our God, and a tenth of our crops to the Levites, since the Levites collect the tithes in all the towns where we work the soil.

A priest, a descendant of Aaron, is to be with the Levites when they collect the tithes, and the Levites are to take a tenth of those tithes up to the house of our God, to the rooms of the storehouse.

For into the storerooms the sons of Israel and the sons of Levi are to bring the contribution of grain, new wine, and oil; there are the holy vessels, and the priests who serve, the gatekeepers, and the singers. We will not forsake the house of our God.

notes.text: Hebrew “Upon the sealed ones (were).”
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has Nobai.
Hebrew Adonai, with the suffix “our.”
See Exodus 23:10–11; Deuteronomy 15:1–2.
Hebrew “a third of a shekel,” about ⅛ ounce (4 grams). Exodus 30:13 had required half a shekel.
Or “dough.”

verses.text: The leaders of the people settled in Jerusalem, and the rest of the people cast lots so that one in ten would come to dwell in Jerusalem the holy city and nine in ten in the towns.
And the people blessed all the men who willingly offered to live in Jerusalem.

These are the heads of the province who lived in Jerusalem; but in the towns of Judah each lived on his own property in their towns: Israel, the priests, the Levites, the temple servants, and the sons of Solomon’s servants.{a}
Some of the people of Judah and Benjamin lived in Jerusalem. From Judah: Athaiah son of Uzziah, son of Zechariah, son of Amariah, son of Shephatiah, son of Mahalalel, a descendant of Perez;
and Maaseiah son of Baruch, son of Col-hozeh, son of Hazaiah, son of Adaiah, son of Joiarib, son of Zechariah, son of the Shilonite.{b}
All the sons of Perez who lived in Jerusalem were 468 valiant men.
And these are the sons of Benjamin: Sallu son of Meshullam, son of Joed, son of Pedaiah, son of Kolaiah, son of Maaseiah, son of Ithiel, son of Jeshaiah,
and after him Gabbai and Sallai,{c} 928.
Joel son of Zichri was overseer over them, and Judah son of Hassenuah was second in charge over the city.
Of the priests: Jedaiah son of Joiarib, Jachin,
Seraiah, son of Hilkiah, son of Meshullam, son of Zadok, son of Meraioth, son of Ahitub, the official in charge of God’s house,
and their brothers who did the work of the house, 822; and Adaiah son of Jeroham, son of Pelaliah, son of Amzi, son of Zechariah, son of Pashhur, son of Malchijah,
with his brothers, heads of fathers’ houses, 242; and Amashsai son of Azarel, son of Ahzai, son of Meshillemoth, son of Immer,
and their brothers, valiant warriors, 128. Their overseer was Zabdiel son of Haggedolim.{d}
And of the Levites: Shemaiah son of Hasshub, son of Azrikam, son of Hashabiah, son of Bunni;
Shabbethai and Jozabad, from the heads of the Levites, over the outer work for the house of God;

Mattaniah son of Mica, son of Zabdi, son of Asaph, the leader who started the thanksgiving prayer; Bakbukiah, who ranked second among his relatives; and Abda son of Shammua, son of Galal, son of Jeduthun.{e}
All the Levites in the holy city were 284.
The gatekeepers, Akkub, Talmon, and their brothers, who kept watch at the gates, were 172.
And the rest of Israel, and of the priests and the Levites, were in all the towns of Judah, each in his inheritance.
But the temple servants lived on the Ophel; and Ziha and Gishpa were over the temple servants.

The chief officer of the Levites in Jerusalem was Uzzi son of Bani, son of Hashabiah, son of Mattaniah, son of Mica, from the descendants of Asaph, the singers responsible for the service of God’s house.
For there was a command from the king concerning them, and a settled provision for the singers, as each day required.
And Pethahiah son of Meshezabel, of the sons of Zerah son of Judah, was at the king’s hand{f} in all matters concerning the people.
As for the villages with their fields, some of the people of Judah lived in Kiriath-arba{g} and its surrounding villages,{h} in Dibon and its villages, and in Jekabzeel and its villages,
and in Jeshua and in Moladah and Beth-pelet,
in Hazar-shual, in Beersheba and its villages,
in Ziklag, in Meconah and its villages,
in En-rimmon, in Zorah, in Jarmuth,
Zanoah, Adullam, and their villages; Lachish with its fields; and Azekah with its villages. They settled from Beersheba all the way to the Valley of Hinnom.
The Benjaminites lived from Geba onward,{i} in Michmash, Aija, and Bethel with its villages,
Anathoth, Nob, Ananiah,
Hazor, Ramah, Gittaim,
Hadid, Zeboim, Neballat,
Lod, and Ono, the valley of craftsmen.{j}
And certain divisions of the Levites that were in Judah were joined to Benjamin.

notes.text: The list in verses 3–19 has a close parallel in 1 Chronicles 9:2–17, with many differences.
Or “of the Shelanite,” a descendant of Shelah son of Judah (Numbers 26:20).
The Hebrew is uncertain; some read “and his brothers, valiant men.”
Or “son of the great ones,” that is, of a leading family.
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has Jedithun.
That is, the king’s agent or adviser for the affairs of the Jews.
The older name of Hebron (Genesis 23:2), “town of four” or “town of Arba.”
Hebrew “daughters.” Likewise in verses 27, 28, 30, and 31.
Or “The sons of Benjamin from Geba lived at Michmash….”
Hebrew Ge-harashim.

verses.text: These are the priests and Levites who came up with Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, and with Jeshua: Seraiah, Jeremiah, and Ezra,
Amariah, Malluch, and Hattush,
Shecaniah, Rehum, and Meremoth,
Iddo, Ginnethoi, and Abijah,
Mijamin, Maadiah, and Bilgah,
Shemaiah, Joiarib, and Jedaiah,
Sallu, Amok, Hilkiah, and Jedaiah. These were the leaders of the priests and their fellow priests in the time of Jeshua.
The Levites were Jeshua, Binnui, Kadmiel, Sherebiah, Judah, and Mattaniah; he and his brothers had charge of the thanksgiving songs.
Bakbukiah and Unni,{a} their brothers, stood across from them by divisions.{b}
Jeshua fathered Joiakim; Joiakim fathered Eliashib; and Eliashib fathered Joiada;
Joiada fathered Jonathan; and Jonathan fathered Jaddua.{c}
And in the days of Joiakim were priests, heads of fathers’ houses: of Seraiah, Meraiah; of Jeremiah, Hananiah;
of Ezra, Meshullam; of Amariah, Jehohanan;
of Melicu,{d} Jonathan; of Shebaniah, Joseph;
of Harim, Adna; of Meraioth, Helkai;
of Iddo,{e} Zechariah; of Ginnethon, Meshullam;
of Abijah, Zichri; of Miniamin,{f} of Moadiah, Piltai;
of Bilgah, Shammua; of Shemaiah, Jehonathan;
of Joiarib, Mattenai; of Jedaiah, Uzzi;
of Sallai, Kallai; of Amok, Eber;
of Hilkiah, Hashabiah; of Jedaiah, Nethanel.
As for the Levites in the days of Eliashib, Joiada, Johanan, and Jaddua, heads of fathers’ houses were written down, and the priests as well, up to the reign of Darius the Persian.{g}
The family heads of the descendants of Levi were recorded in the Book of the Chronicles up to the time of Johanan son of Eliashib.

The leaders of the Levites were Hashabiah, Sherebiah, and Jeshua son of Kadmiel, along with their fellow Levites, who stood opposite them to give praise and thanks, one group answering the other, as David the man of God had commanded.
Mattaniah, Bakbukiah, Obadiah, Meshullam, Talmon, and Akkub were gatekeepers who guarded the storerooms at the gates.
These were in the days of Joiakim son of Jeshua, son of Jozadak, and in the days of Nehemiah the governor and of Ezra the priest, the scribe.

For the dedication of Jerusalem’s wall they searched out the Levites wherever they lived and brought them to Jerusalem to keep the dedication joyfully, with songs of thanks and with music on cymbals, harps, and lyres.
And the sons of the singers gathered together from the surrounding district around Jerusalem and from the villages of the Netophathites,
and from Beth-gilgal and the fields of Geba and Azmaveth, since the singers had made villages for themselves around Jerusalem.
And the priests and the Levites purified themselves, and they purified the people and the gates and the wall.
I had the officials of Judah go up on top of the wall, and I set two large thanksgiving choirs in procession. One went along the top of the wall southward,{h} toward the Dung Gate;
And after them went Hoshaiah and half of the leaders of Judah,
and Azariah, Ezra, Meshullam,
Judah, Benjamin, Shemaiah, and Jeremiah,
and some of the priests’ sons with trumpets: Zechariah son of Jonathan, son of Shemaiah, son of Mattaniah, son of Micaiah, son of Zaccur, son of Asaph;
and his brothers, Shemaiah, Azarel, Milalai, Gilalai, Maai, Nethanel, Judah, and Hanani, with the musical instruments of David the man of God. And Ezra the scribe went before them.
At the Fountain Gate they climbed straight up the steps of the City of David, on the rising part of the wall above David’s palace, and went on to the Water Gate on the east.
The second thanksgiving choir went northward,{i} with me following and half the people, on top of the wall, beyond the Tower of the Ovens to the Broad Wall,
over the Gate of Ephraim, past the Old Gate,{j} by the Fish Gate and Hananel’s Tower and the Tower of the Hundred, to the Sheep Gate; and they took their stand at the Gate of the Guard.
So both choirs that gave thanks stood in the house of God, and I and half of the officials with me;
and the priests Eliakim, Maaseiah, Miniamin, Micaiah, Elioenai, Zechariah, and Hananiah, with trumpets;
and Maaseiah, Shemaiah, Eleazar, Uzzi, Jehohanan, Malchijah, Elam, and Ezer. And the singers sang aloud, with Jezrahiah as their leader.
On that day they offered great sacrifices and rejoiced, because God had given them great joy. The women and children rejoiced too, and the sound of Jerusalem’s celebration was heard far away.

On that day men were appointed over the storerooms for the contributions, the firstfruits, and the tithes. They were to gather into them, from the fields around the towns, the portions required by the Law for the priests and Levites, because the people of Judah were pleased with the priests and Levites who served.
They performed the charge of their God and the charge of cleansing, and so did the singers and gatekeepers, as David and Solomon his son had commanded.
For in David’s day, and Asaph’s, long before, there were chiefs{k} over the singers, and songs of praise and thanks to God.

And all Israel in the days of Zerubbabel and in the days of Nehemiah gave the portions for the singers and the gatekeepers, as each day required. And they set apart that which was for the Levites, and the Levites set apart that which was for the sons of Aaron.

notes.text: So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has Unno.
Or “by watches”; Hebrew “for watches.”

Jaddua was high priest about 330 BC, according to Josephus. The Jonathan of this verse is probably the Johanan of verses 22–23 (see the Elephantine papyri, which name a high priest Johanan about 410 BC).
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has Malluchi. Compare Malluch in verse 2.
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has Iddi.
A name seems to have dropped out of the Hebrew text here.
Probably Darius II, king of Persia 423–404 BC, though some think of Darius III (336–330 BC).
Hebrew “to the right,” that is, to the south for one facing east.
Hebrew “to the front,” perhaps “opposite”; the Septuagint and other ancient versions read “to the left,” that is, to the north.
Or “the Jeshanah Gate”; see 3:6.
So the traditional reading (qere); the written text (ketiv) has the singular, “a head.”

verses.text: On that day the Book of Moses was read aloud to the people, and in it they found it written that an Ammonite or a Moabite must never come into the assembly of God,
because they had not met the Israelites with food and water, but had hired Balaam to curse them. Yet our God turned the curse into a blessing.{a}
When the people heard the Law, they set apart from Israel everyone of foreign mixture.
Now before this, Eliashib the priest, who was appointed over the chambers of the house of our God, and who was related to Tobiah,

had made ready for him a great room, where before they used to store the grain offering, the frankincense, and the vessels, with the tithe of grain, new wine, and oil commanded for the Levites, singers, and gatekeepers, and the contributions due the priests.
I was not in Jerusalem while all this was happening, because in the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes king of Babylon{b} I had gone back to the king. Some time later I asked the king for leave
When I came to Jerusalem I learned of the wrong Eliashib had done for Tobiah in fitting out a room for him in the courts of God’s house.
It displeased me deeply, and I flung all of Tobiah’s household goods out of the room.
At my command they purified the rooms, and I put back in them the vessels of God’s house along with the grain offering and the frankincense.
I also learned that the Levites had not been given their share, so that the Levites and singers who did the work had each gone back to his own farm.
I rebuked the officials and asked, “Why has the house of God been neglected?” Then I gathered the Levites and singers and restored them to their posts.
And all Judah brought in the tithe of grain, new wine, and oil to the storerooms.

Over the storerooms I put in charge Shelemiah the priest, Zadok the scribe, and Pedaiah from the Levites, with Hanan son of Zaccur, son of Mattaniah, to help them, since they were counted trustworthy; it fell to them to hand out shares to their brothers.
Remember me, O my God, concerning this, and do not wipe out my good deeds that I have done for the house of my God and for its services.

In those days I saw men in Judah treading the winepresses on the Sabbath, bringing in sheaves and loading donkeys with them, and with wine, grapes, figs, and every sort of burden, bringing them into Jerusalem on the Sabbath day. And I testified against them on the day they sold provisions.
Tyrians who lived there also brought in fish and every kind of merchandise and sold it on the Sabbath to the people of Judah, even in Jerusalem.
Then I confronted the nobles of Judah and said to them, “What is this evil thing that you are doing, profaning the Sabbath day?
Is this not what your fathers did, so that our God brought all this evil on us and on this city? And you add to the wrath on Israel by profaning the Sabbath!”

When the gates of Jerusalem grew shadowed before the Sabbath, I gave word and the doors were shut, and I ordered that they not be opened until the Sabbath was over. I set some of my young men over the gates so that no burden would come in on the Sabbath day.
The traders and the sellers of all sorts of wares then lodged outside Jerusalem, once and twice.
But I warned them and said to them, “Why are you lodging in front of the wall? If you do so again, I will lay hands on you.” From that time on they did not come on the Sabbath.

And I told the Levites to purify themselves and come to keep the gates, so as to hallow the Sabbath day. For this, too, remember me, my God, and have pity on me as befits your abundant steadfast love.
In those days also I saw the Jews who had married women of Ashdod, Ammon, and Moab.{c}
Half of their children spoke Ashdodite, and none of them knew how to speak Judean,{d} only the tongue of one people or another.

I contended with them and cursed them; I struck some of the men and tore out their hair, and I put them under oath by God: “Do not give your daughters to their sons, and do not take any of their daughters for your sons or yourselves.

Didn’t Solomon king of Israel sin because of women like these? Among the many nations there was no king like him. He was loved by his God, and God made him king over all Israel. Yet even he was drawn into sin by foreign women.{e}
And must we hear of you doing all this great evil, being faithless to our God by marrying foreign women?”
One of the sons of Joiada son of Eliashib the high priest was son-in-law to Sanballat the Horonite, so I drove him away from me.
Remember them, O my God, because they have defiled the priesthood and the covenant of the priesthood and the Levites.
So I purified them from everything foreign and set up the duties for the priests and the Levites, each man in his task,
and I provided for the wood offering at appointed times, and for the firstfruits. Remember me, O my God, for good.
